Reframed through the lens of the monetary economics literature, the December 16, 2020 FOMC statement is notably dovish and supportive. The Fed’s outcome-based forward guidance—holding the funds rate at 0–0.25% until maximum employment is reached and inflation both reaches 2% and is on track to moderately exceed 2%—embeds the average-inflation “makeup” strategy Chair Powell announced at Jackson Hole 2020. This aligns with the inflation-forecast targeting framework (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) and New Keynesian insights that managing expectations is central to stabilizing the economy. At the zero lower bound, the combination of explicit guidance and large-scale asset purchases ($80B Treasuries and $40B agency MBS per month) is consistent with the literature on forward guidance and quantitative easing as effective tools to lower term premia, ease financial conditions, and support credit intermediation when conventional policy is constrained. The statement acknowledges substantial pandemic-related downside risks—consistent with evidence of elevated economic policy uncertainty and supply-demand shocks during COVID-19—but, relative to a simple Taylor-rule baseline, the AIT framework and continued QE indicate a stronger commitment to accommodative policy that should lift inflation expectations toward target and support the recovery.

Net assessment: while the health crisis weighs on the near-term outlook, the policy stance—grounded in established research on expectations, the zero lower bound, and QE—tilts the overall tone slightly positive.
